subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Tom Mitchell's definition of machine learning
question: According to Tom Mitchell's definition, when is a computer program said to 'learn'? Give an example with a spam filter.
reference_answer: According to Mitchell, a program is said to learn from experience E with respect to a class of tasks T and performance measure P if its performance on tasks in T, as measured by P, improves with experience E. Spam filter example: T is classifying emails as spam or not spam; E is the set of emails labeled by users; P is the proportion of correctly classified emails.
key_points: Learning means improving performance P on task T through experience E
Spam filter: T is classification, E is labeled emails, P is the accuracy

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: In supervised learning, what are 'features' and 'labels'? Give an example with house price prediction.
reference_answer: Features are the input attributes describing a data sample, used by the model to make predictions. The label is the correct output value the model must learn to predict. For house price prediction, features may be area, number of bedrooms, location, age of the house; the label is the actual sale price.
key_points: Features are input attributes describing a sample
The label is the correct output to predict; e.g., the house price

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Distinguish the parameters and the hyperparameters of a machine learning model.
reference_answer: Parameters are values the model LEARNS from data during training, e.g., the weights and bias of linear regression or a neural network. Hyperparameters are values SET BY the designer before training to control the learning process or model structure, e.g., the learning rate, number of hidden layers, number of trees in a Random Forest, k in k-NN, regularization strength. Hyperparameters are usually chosen by experimenting on a validation set.
key_points: Parameters are learned from data (weights, bias)
Hyperparameters are set beforehand to control learning (learning rate, layers, k); chosen via a validation set

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: How do a loss function and a cost function differ?
reference_answer: A loss function measures how wrong a prediction is on ONE data sample, e.g., (y_pred - y_true)² for one house. A cost function aggregates (usually averages) the loss over the ENTIRE training set, possibly plus a regularization term; this is the quantity the optimization algorithm tries to minimize. Many sources use the two terms interchangeably.
key_points: Loss measures error on one sample
Cost is the average loss over the whole set (possibly with regularization), the objective to minimize

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: What is the basic idea of the Gradient Descent algorithm?
reference_answer: Gradient Descent finds parameter values minimizing the cost function iteratively: compute the gradient (partial derivatives) of the cost with respect to the parameters — the vector pointing in the direction of steepest increase — then update the parameters in the OPPOSITE direction: θ ← θ - α·∇J(θ), where α is the learning rate. Picture walking downhill in fog: each step goes in the steepest downhill direction, repeating until it can barely decrease further.
key_points: Update parameters opposite to the gradient: θ ← θ - α·∇J(θ)
Repeat until the cost converges; α is the learning rate

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Logistic regression and the sigmoid function
question: Why does logistic regression for classification need the sigmoid function?
reference_answer: Logistic regression computes a linear combination z = w·x + b, but z can be any real number. The sigmoid function σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e^(-z)) squashes z into the range (0, 1), so the output can be interpreted as the PROBABILITY that the sample belongs to the positive class. It is then compared with a threshold (usually 0.5) to decide the class. The sigmoid is also smooth and differentiable, convenient for gradient-based optimization.
key_points: Sigmoid maps any real z into (0, 1), interpreted as a probability
Compared with a threshold (usually 0.5) to classify; differentiable so it can be optimized with gradients

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: What is the decision boundary of a classifier?
reference_answer: The decision boundary is the line (in 2D), plane or hypersurface (in higher dimensions) dividing the feature space into regions corresponding to different classes: points on one side are predicted as one class, points on the other side as another. For logistic regression, the boundary is the set of points where w·x + b = 0 (probability 0.5), a line/hyperplane; with polynomial features or non-linear models (decision trees, neural networks) the boundary can be curved or complex.
key_points: The decision boundary divides feature space into regions by predicted class
Logistic regression has a linear boundary w·x + b = 0; non-linear models produce complex boundaries

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Which cells make up the confusion matrix of a binary classification problem?
reference_answer: The confusion matrix has four cells: True Positive (TP) — predicted positive and actually positive; True Negative (TN) — predicted negative and actually negative; False Positive (FP) — predicted positive but actually negative (false alarm, type I error); False Negative (FN) — predicted negative but actually positive (miss, type II error). Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1 and many other metrics are computed from these four cells.
key_points: Four cells: TP, TN, FP (false alarm), FN (miss)
The basis for Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: What does the ROC curve represent and what does the AUC metric mean?
reference_answer: The ROC curve plots the True Positive Rate (TPR = Recall) against the False Positive Rate (FPR = FP / (FP + TN)) as the classification threshold varies from high to low. AUC (area under the ROC curve) summarizes model quality over all thresholds: AUC = 1 is perfect, 0.5 is equivalent to random guessing. AUC also equals the probability that the model scores a random positive sample higher than a random negative sample.
key_points: ROC plots TPR against FPR as the threshold varies
AUC summarizes discrimination over all thresholds: 1 perfect, 0.5 random

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Why should the feature 'city' (Hanoi, Da Nang, Ho Chi Minh City) not be encoded as the numbers 1, 2, 3 for linear regression? How does one-hot encoding solve this?
reference_answer: Encoding as 1, 2, 3 unintentionally creates an artificial ORDER and DISTANCE: a linear model will treat Ho Chi Minh City as 'greater' than Hanoi and Da Nang as lying 'between' the two cities, which is meaningless. One-hot encoding creates a binary column for each value (is_Hanoi, is_DaNang, is_HCMC), with exactly one column equal to 1 per sample. The values are treated equally and the model learns a separate weight for each city. Drawback: the number of columns grows greatly when the feature has many values.
key_points: Ordinal number encoding creates a fake order/distance between categories
One-hot creates a binary column per value; the drawback is many columns for high-cardinality features

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: List common ways of handling missing values in training data.
reference_answer: (1) Deletion: remove rows with missing values (when few) or drop the entire column (when mostly missing). (2) Statistical imputation: mean or median for numeric features, the most frequent value for categorical features. (3) Model-based imputation: predict missing values from other features (k-NN, regression). (4) Add a 'missing' indicator column, since missingness itself may carry information. The statistics used for imputation must be computed only on the training set and then applied to the test set.
key_points: Delete rows/columns, impute mean/median/mode, or impute with a model
Optionally add a missingness indicator; compute imputation statistics only on the training set

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Distinguish the concepts of epoch, batch size and iteration when training neural networks.
reference_answer: Batch size is the number of samples used to compute the gradient and update the weights once. An iteration (step) is one weight update, i.e., processing one batch. An epoch is one pass of the model through the ENTIRE training set. For example, with 10,000 training samples and batch size 100, each epoch has 100 iterations; training for 20 epochs means 2,000 weight updates.
key_points: Batch size: samples per update; iteration: one update
Epoch: one pass over the whole training set; iterations per epoch = samples / batch size

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Batch, Stochastic and Mini-batch Gradient Descent
question: Compare Batch Gradient Descent, Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) and Mini-batch Gradient Descent.
reference_answer: Batch GD computes the gradient on the ENTIRE dataset for each update: accurate, stable directions but each step is very slow with large data. SGD updates after EACH sample: very fast and the noise can escape some shallow minima, but the path oscillates strongly. Mini-batch GD uses a small group (e.g., 32-512 samples) each time: balancing stability and speed and exploiting parallel computation on GPUs — the most common choice in practice.
key_points: Batch: whole dataset, stable but slow; SGD: one sample, fast but noisy
Mini-batch: small groups, balancing stability and speed, GPU-friendly — most common

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: What is the softmax function at the output layer of a multi-class classification network used for?
reference_answer: Softmax turns a vector of arbitrary real scores (logits) z_1, ..., z_K into a probability distribution over K classes: p_i = e^(z_i) / Σ_j e^(z_j). Each p_i lies in (0, 1) and the p_i sum to 1; classes with higher scores receive higher probabilities, and the exponential amplifies the differences between scores. The predicted class is the one with the highest probability.
key_points: Softmax turns logits into a probability distribution over K classes summing to 1
The exponential amplifies differences; the prediction is the most probable class

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: How is the cross-entropy loss for classification computed and how does it 'penalize' the model?
reference_answer: With a one-hot true label y and predicted probabilities p, cross-entropy is L = -Σ_i y_i·log(p_i), i.e., -log(the probability the model assigns to the correct class). If the model assigns high probability to the correct class (near 1), the loss is near 0; if it assigns very low probability (near 0), -log(p) is very large. Therefore cross-entropy heavily penalizes predictions that are WRONG yet CONFIDENT, encouraging the model to give high probability to the correct class.
key_points: Cross-entropy = -log(predicted probability of the correct class)
Heavily penalizes confident wrong predictions

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: How does early stopping combat overfitting?
reference_answer: During training, monitor the error on the VALIDATION set after each epoch. Initially both training and validation errors decrease; at some point the validation error starts to rise while the training error keeps falling — a sign the model is beginning to memorize noise. Early stopping halts training when the validation error has not improved for a certain number of epochs (patience) and restores the weights from the point of best validation error.
key_points: Monitor validation error and stop when it stops improving for some epochs
Restore the best weights; prevents the model from continuing to memorize noise

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: What is data augmentation in computer vision and why does it help models generalize better?
reference_answer: Data augmentation creates new training samples from existing data using label-preserving transformations: horizontal flips, slight rotations, crops, zooms, brightness/color changes, added noise. A horizontally flipped cat is still a cat. The model thus sees more variations, learns features invariant to those changes, and overfits less when data is scarce. Transformations must be chosen appropriately — e.g., do not flip the digit 6 upside down into a 9.
key_points: Create new samples with label-preserving transformations (flip, rotate, crop, color)
Makes models invariant to transformations and reduces overfitting; transformations must not change the label

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: How does a Recurrent Neural Network differ from a feedforward network, and what kind of data is it suited for?
reference_answer: An RNN processes sequential data step by step and maintains a 'hidden state' passed from one step to the next: h_t = f(W·x_t + U·h_(t-1) + b). The hidden state acts as a memory summarizing what has been seen, and the same set of weights is used at every time step. Thus RNNs handle variable-length sequences such as text, speech and time series — whereas feedforward networks only accept fixed-size inputs and have no memory.
key_points: An RNN keeps a hidden state passed across time steps, sharing weights
Suited for variable-length sequential data: text, speech, time series

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Which components does an LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory) add compared to a simple RNN?
reference_answer: An LSTM adds a 'cell state' running along the sequence and three sigmoid-controlled gates: the forget gate decides how much old information to erase from the cell; the input gate decides how much new information to write; the output gate decides which part of the cell is exposed as the hidden state. Thanks to the gates and cell updates done mainly by addition, LSTMs remember much longer dependencies than simple RNNs.
key_points: An LSTM has a cell state and three gates: forget, input, output
Gates regulate reading/writing/erasing, enabling long-range memory

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: What does a pooling layer in a CNN do? Distinguish max pooling and average pooling.
reference_answer: A pooling layer reduces the spatial size of feature maps by summarizing small regions (e.g., 2×2) into one value: max pooling takes the LARGEST value in the region (keeping the most prominent feature), average pooling takes the MEAN. Pooling reduces computation and parameters in later layers, enlarges the receptive field, and provides a small degree of invariance to shifts in feature position.
key_points: Pooling shrinks feature maps by summarizing small regions
Max takes the largest value, average the mean; reduces computation and adds small shift invariance

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Distinguish generative models and discriminative models.
reference_answer: A discriminative model directly learns the boundary between classes, i.e., the conditional probability P(y | x) — answering 'given this input, what is the label'. Examples: logistic regression, SVMs, most classification networks. A generative model learns how the data is produced, i.e., the distributions P(x | y) and P(y) (or P(x)), from which P(y | x) can be derived via Bayes' theorem and new data samples can be GENERATED. Examples: Naive Bayes, Hidden Markov Models, GANs, language models.
key_points: Discriminative: learns P(y | x), focusing on boundaries (logistic regression, SVM)
Generative: learns data distributions P(x | y), P(x), can generate new samples (Naive Bayes, GANs, LLMs)

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Which components make up a Generative Adversarial Network and on what principle does it work?
reference_answer: A GAN consists of two networks trained adversarially: the Generator takes random noise and produces fake data (e.g., face images); the Discriminator receives both real and fake data and tries to tell them apart. The Generator is trained to fool the Discriminator, while the Discriminator is trained not to be fooled — like a game between a counterfeiter and the police. At equilibrium, the Generator produces data very similar to real data.
key_points: A Generator produces fake data and a Discriminator distinguishes real from fake
Adversarial training like a two-player game; at equilibrium generated data looks real

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: What is an autoencoder and what are its applications?
reference_answer: An autoencoder is a neural network that learns to reconstruct its own input through a 'bottleneck': the encoder compresses the input into a low-dimensional representation (latent code), the decoder reconstructs the input from it; it is trained to minimize the difference between output and input, without labels. Applications: dimensionality reduction/compression, image denoising (denoising autoencoders), anomaly detection (anomalous samples have large reconstruction errors), representation learning, and the VAE variant for data generation.
key_points: The encoder compresses input into a low-dimensional code, the decoder reconstructs it; trained without labels
Applications: dimensionality reduction, denoising, anomaly detection, representation learning, generation (VAE)

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Large language models: pre-training and fine-tuning
question: Large language models (LLMs) are usually built in two stages: pre-training and fine-tuning. What does each stage do?
reference_answer: Pre-training: the model is trained on an enormous amount of text (trillions of tokens) with a self-supervised task — predicting the next token — learning grammar, world knowledge and general reasoning abilities; this stage requires massive compute. Fine-tuning: further training on smaller, high-quality datasets for specific purposes, e.g., following instructions (instruction tuning), safe and helpful conversation (often combined with learning from human feedback), or domain specialization.
key_points: Pre-training: next-token prediction on huge data, learning general knowledge
Fine-tuning: smaller high-quality data for instruction following, safety or domain specialization

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Distinguish using a language model in a zero-shot versus a few-shot manner.
reference_answer: Zero-shot: describe the task in words without any examples, e.g., 'Classify the sentiment of the following sentence as positive or negative: ...'. Few-shot: include a few example demonstrations (inputs and desired outputs) directly in the prompt before the input to process; the model infers the format and pattern from the examples — called in-context learning. Neither updates the model's weights. Few-shot usually improves accuracy and output format consistency.
key_points: Zero-shot: only a task description, no examples
Few-shot: a few examples in the prompt (in-context learning), no weight updates

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Modern language models process text in units called 'tokens'. Why do they use subword tokenization (e.g., BPE) instead of splitting by words or characters?
reference_answer: Word-level tokenization requires a huge vocabulary and cannot handle new words, typos or proper names (out-of-vocabulary words). Character-level tokenization has a small vocabulary but very long sequences, making meaning harder to learn and costing more compute. Subword tokenization (like Byte-Pair Encoding) is a balance: common words are single tokens, rare words are split into common pieces (e.g., 'unhappiness' → 'un', 'happi', 'ness'), so the vocabulary is moderate (tens of thousands) while any string can be represented. BPE is built by repeatedly merging the most frequent pair of symbols.
key_points: Word-level cannot handle new words; character-level makes sequences too long
Subword (BPE) balances: common words are one token, rare words split into pieces; moderate vocabulary

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Distinguish three computer vision tasks: image classification, object detection and image segmentation.
reference_answer: Image classification: assign ONE label to the whole image (this image is a 'cat'). Object detection: locate each object with a bounding box plus a label (there are 2 cats and 1 dog at these coordinates). Segmentation: assign a label to EACH PIXEL — semantic segmentation distinguishes classes (which pixels are cat, which are background), instance segmentation also distinguishes individual objects (the first and second cat). Detail and difficulty increase in that order.
key_points: Classification: one label per image; detection: bounding box + label for each object
Segmentation: a label per pixel (semantic or instance)

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Recommender systems: collaborative filtering and content-based
question: Distinguish two approaches of recommender systems: collaborative filtering and content-based recommendation.
reference_answer: Collaborative filtering relies on the behavior of MANY users: 'people with tastes like yours also liked this product' — it does not need to know product content and can make interesting serendipitous suggestions, but suffers from the cold start problem with new users/products lacking interactions. Content-based recommendation uses product features (genre, actors, keywords) and the user's own preference profile: 'you like action movies, so here is another action movie' — it can recommend new products but tends to be monotonous with little discovery. Real systems usually combine both (hybrid).
key_points: Collaborative filtering: based on similar users' behavior, suffers from cold start
Content-based: based on item features and personal preferences, can be monotonous; real systems are often hybrid

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: What is anomaly detection? Why is it often approached with unsupervised learning?
reference_answer: Anomaly detection identifies data samples that differ significantly from the majority of 'normal' data, e.g., fraudulent transactions, machine faults from sensor data, network intrusions. Anomalies are usually very RARE, diverse and may be of never-seen-before kinds, so collecting enough labels for every type is hard. Therefore one typically models the distribution of normal data (Gaussian density estimation, Isolation Forest, autoencoders) and flags samples with low probability or high reconstruction error as anomalous.
key_points: Detects samples significantly different from normal data (fraud, equipment faults)
Anomalies are rare and diverse, so model normal data and flag low-probability samples

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Which components define a Markov Decision Process?
reference_answer: An MDP consists of: a set of states S; a set of actions A; a transition function P(s' | s, a) — the probability of reaching state s' when taking action a in state s; a reward function R(s, a, s'); and a discount factor γ. Markov property: the next state and reward depend only on the current state and action, not on earlier history. MDPs are the standard mathematical framework for reinforcement learning and sequential decision making in stochastic environments.
key_points: Components: states, actions, transition probabilities, rewards, discount factor
Markov property: the future depends only on the current state and action

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: What does the discount factor γ (0 ≤ γ ≤ 1) mean in reinforcement learning? What happens when γ is close to 0 and when it is close to 1?
reference_answer: The return is computed as G = r_1 + γ·r_2 + γ²·r_3 + ..., so rewards far in the future are discounted exponentially. γ close to 0: the agent is 'myopic', caring almost only about immediate rewards. γ close to 1: the agent is 'far-sighted', valuing long-term rewards nearly as much as current ones. γ < 1 also guarantees a finite return in problems without a terminal state, and reflects uncertainty about the future.
key_points: γ discounts future rewards exponentially
γ near 0: myopic; near 1: far-sighted; γ < 1 keeps returns finite

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: What is a policy in reinforcement learning? Distinguish deterministic and stochastic policies.
reference_answer: A policy is the agent's behavioral strategy: a mapping from states to actions. A deterministic policy π(s) = a always chooses a fixed action for each state. A stochastic policy π(a | s) gives the probability of choosing each action in state s — useful for exploration, and in adversarial games (like rock-paper-scissors) a stochastic policy can beat every deterministic one. The goal of reinforcement learning is to find an optimal policy maximizing the expected total reward.
key_points: A policy maps states to actions
Deterministic: a fixed action; stochastic: a probability distribution over actions

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: The Manhattan distance heuristic for the 8-puzzle
question: For the 8-puzzle (3×3 sliding tile puzzle), how is the 'sum of Manhattan distances' heuristic computed and why is it admissible?
reference_answer: For each numbered tile (not the blank), compute the Manhattan distance between its current and goal positions: |current row - goal row| + |current column - goal column|; the heuristic is the sum of these distances. It is admissible (never overestimates the true cost) because each move shifts EXACTLY ONE tile by exactly one step, so each tile needs at least its Manhattan distance in moves to reach its goal. This heuristic dominates the 'number of misplaced tiles' heuristic, so A* expands fewer nodes with it.
key_points: Sum of |Δrow| + |Δcolumn| of each tile relative to its goal position
Admissible because each move shifts one tile one step; it dominates the misplaced-tiles heuristic

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: What is an ontology in knowledge representation?
reference_answer: An ontology is a formal, explicit specification of the CONCEPTS in a domain, their PROPERTIES and the RELATIONSHIPS among them (e.g., 'a Doctor is a Person', 'a Doctor treats Patients', 'a Hospital has Departments'). Ontologies provide a shared vocabulary so humans and computers can share, integrate and reason over knowledge consistently. Examples: SNOMED CT in medicine, ontologies written in the OWL language of the Semantic Web.
key_points: An ontology formally specifies a domain's concepts, properties and relationships
Provides a shared vocabulary for sharing, integrating and reasoning (SNOMED CT, OWL)

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: How does fuzzy logic differ from classical logic? Give an example.
reference_answer: In classical logic, a proposition can only be true (1) or false (0). Fuzzy logic allows DEGREES of membership in [0, 1]: e.g., a temperature of 28°C may belong to the set 'hot' with degree 0.6 and 'warm' with degree 0.4. Rules like 'IF temperature is hot THEN increase fan speed' are applied according to these degrees, then combined and defuzzified to produce a concrete control value. Fuzzy logic suits the vague concepts of human language and is used in washing machine, air conditioner and braking system controllers.
key_points: Fuzzy logic allows degrees of truth in [0, 1] instead of only true/false
Linguistic rules are applied by degree; used in device control

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: In the STRIPS representation for automated planning, which components describe an action?
reference_answer: Each STRIPS action consists of: a name and parameters; preconditions — the set of propositions that must be true in the current state for the action to be executed; an add list — propositions that become true after the action; a delete list — propositions that become false after the action. Example PickUp(x): preconditions HandEmpty and OnTable(x); add Holding(x); delete HandEmpty and OnTable(x). A state is a set of true propositions; any proposition not mentioned remains unchanged.
key_points: A STRIPS action has preconditions, an add list and a delete list
A state is a set of true propositions; unmentioned propositions stay unchanged

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: The lifecycle of a machine learning project
question: What are the main steps of a typical machine learning project (according to the 'AI For Everyone' course)?
reference_answer: (1) Define the problem and business goal, and check feasibility; (2) collect data — determine the data needed, label it; (3) train the model — iterate many times trying models, evaluating, adjusting; (4) deploy the model into a real product; (5) monitor and maintain — track performance, collect new real-world data and retrain when data changes. It is an iterative process, not a one-time linear one.
key_points: Steps: define the problem, collect data, train, deploy, monitor
An iterative process: new real-world data is fed back to improve and retrain

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Why does label quality strongly affect supervised learning models? How can label quality be ensured?
reference_answer: Supervised models learn from the labels provided; wrong or inconsistent labels (two annotators interpreting the same case differently) teach the model incorrectly, lower accuracy and make evaluation unreliable. Ways to ensure quality: write clear labeling guidelines with examples for hard cases; have multiple annotators label the same samples and measure agreement; have domain experts review difficult samples; perform periodic random audits; and fix wrong labels found during error analysis.
key_points: Wrong or inconsistent labels teach the model incorrectly and make evaluation unreliable
Ensure quality with clear guidelines, annotator agreement, expert review, periodic audits

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: What is Explainable AI (XAI) and why is it important?
reference_answer: XAI is a set of methods helping humans understand WHY an AI model made a particular decision, e.g., showing which features most influenced a loan rejection, or which image regions led to a diagnosis. It matters because it: builds user trust; helps detect errors, biases and spurious correlations; meets legal requirements regarding the right to explanation for decisions affecting people; and supports experts (doctors, underwriters) in deciding whether to trust the model.
key_points: XAI helps humans understand why a model made a decision
Important for trust, detecting errors/bias, legal compliance, and supporting experts

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: What is data anonymization and why is removing names and national ID numbers often not enough?
reference_answer: Anonymization processes data so the individuals it describes cannot be identified. Removing only direct identifiers (names, national IDs, phone numbers) is often insufficient because 'quasi-identifiers' combined can still uniquely identify a person: e.g., date of birth + gender + postal code suffices to identify most of a population; data can also be linked with other public sources. Additional techniques: generalization (keeping only the birth year, broader regions), k-anonymity (each record identical to at least k - 1 others), and adding noise via differential privacy.
key_points: Anonymization aims to make individuals unidentifiable from data
Combined quasi-identifiers can still identify people; use generalization, k-anonymity, differential privacy

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Distinguish using AI to 'automate' versus to 'augment' human work. Give examples.
reference_answer: Automation: AI fully performs a task previously done by humans, e.g., automatically classifying emails, reading invoice numbers, chatbots answering FAQs. Augmentation: AI helps humans do better and faster while the final decision remains human, e.g., AI highlighting suspicious regions on X-rays for doctors to review, code suggestions for programmers. AI usually automates individual TASKS rather than entire JOBS; many jobs will be restructured toward humans working together with AI.
key_points: Automation: AI performs tasks instead of humans
Augmentation: AI assists while humans make the final decision; AI usually automates tasks, not whole jobs

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: How does forward propagation work in a multi-layer neural network?
reference_answer: Input data passes through the network layer by layer from input to output. At each layer l, each neuron computes a weighted sum of the previous layer's outputs plus a bias: z^(l) = W^(l)·a^(l-1) + b^(l), then applies an activation function: a^(l) = g(z^(l)). The output of the last layer is the network's prediction (e.g., probabilities via softmax). Forward propagation is used both for prediction and during training (to compute the loss, followed by backpropagation to compute gradients).
key_points: Each layer computes z = W·a_prev + b then a = g(z), from input to output
Used for prediction and to compute the loss before backpropagation

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Why can a single-layer perceptron not learn the XOR function? How is this overcome?
reference_answer: A single-layer perceptron produces a decision boundary that is a straight line (hyperplane), so it can only classify LINEARLY SEPARABLE data. For XOR, the points (0,0), (1,1) output 0 and (0,1), (1,0) output 1, lying diagonally — no straight line can separate the two groups. This observation by Minsky and Papert (1969) contributed to the first AI winter. Solution: use a multi-layer network with a hidden layer and non-linear activations — the hidden layer transforms the space so the data becomes linearly separable (e.g., XOR = (x1 OR x2) AND NOT (x1 AND x2)).
key_points: A single-layer perceptron has only linear boundaries; XOR is not linearly separable
A multi-layer network with hidden layers and non-linear activations solves XOR

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: The role of the bias term
question: What role does the bias b play in the neuron formula y = g(w·x + b)?
reference_answer: Without a bias, the sum w·x is always 0 when all inputs are 0, and the decision boundary w·x = 0 must pass through the origin. The bias allows SHIFTING the activation function left/right (or moving the decision boundary away from the origin), like the intercept in the line equation y = ax + b. This makes the neuron more flexible in fitting data, e.g., deciding to 'activate when the total input exceeds some threshold' rather than only when it exceeds 0.
key_points: The bias shifts the activation function/decision boundary away from the origin
Like the intercept of a line, it increases flexibility when fitting data

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Why is cosine similarity commonly used to compare embedding vectors of words or sentences?
reference_answer: Cosine similarity = (a·b) / (‖a‖·‖b‖) measures the angle between two vectors, ranging from -1 to 1: near 1 means the same direction (similar meaning), near 0 means unrelated. It only considers DIRECTION, not vector LENGTH, which suits embedding spaces where direction encodes meaning while length is often influenced by factors such as word frequency or text length. Cosine is used in semantic search, finding similar documents and RAG systems.
key_points: Cosine measures the angle between two vectors, from -1 to 1
Ignores length and considers direction, which encodes meaning; used in semantic search

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: The elbow method for choosing the number of clusters
question: How does the elbow method help choose the number of clusters k for K-Means? What are its limitations?
reference_answer: Run K-Means with several k values (1, 2, 3, ...) and compute the sum of squared distances from points to their cluster centers (WCSS/inertia). WCSS always decreases as k increases (k = n gives 0), so we cannot simply choose the k with the smallest WCSS. Plot WCSS against k and choose the 'elbow' point — where increasing k further no longer reduces WCSS significantly. Limitations: often the plot has no clear elbow, so the choice is subjective; combine it with other metrics (silhouette) and domain knowledge.
key_points: Plot WCSS against k and choose the point where further increases barely reduce WCSS
WCSS always decreases with k; the elbow may be unclear, so combine with silhouette and domain knowledge

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Describe how agglomerative hierarchical clustering builds a dendrogram from data, and when it should be chosen instead of K-Means.
reference_answer: Initially each point is its own cluster; repeatedly merge the TWO CLOSEST CLUSTERS into one until only one cluster remains. The distance between two clusters is defined by a linkage method: single (closest pair of points), complete (farthest pair), average (mean), Ward (smallest increase in variance). The result is a hierarchical tree (dendrogram); cutting it at some height yields the desired number of clusters. Advantages: no need to choose k beforehand, reveals hierarchical structure, can find arbitrarily shaped clusters (with single linkage). Drawbacks: costly, O(n²) memory or more, hard to apply to very large data.
key_points: Start with each point as a cluster, repeatedly merge the two closest, forming a dendrogram
No need to choose k beforehand, shows hierarchy; but costly and hard to scale

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: What is feature selection and what benefits does it bring?
reference_answer: Feature selection chooses a subset of the most useful features from the original feature set, removing irrelevant or redundant ones. Method families: filter (based on statistics such as correlation, mutual information), wrapper (trying subsets with a model), embedded (selection during training, like L1 driving weights to 0). Benefits: less overfitting, simpler and more interpretable models, faster training and prediction, lower data collection cost. Unlike PCA, feature selection preserves the meaning of the original features.
key_points: Choose a useful subset of features; filter, wrapper, embedded (L1) methods
Reduces overfitting, improves interpretability and speed; preserves original feature meaning

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Which four criteria are search algorithms usually evaluated by?
reference_answer: (1) Completeness: is the algorithm guaranteed to find a solution if one exists? (2) Optimality: is the found solution the lowest-cost one? (3) Time complexity: the number of nodes generated/expanded, usually expressed in terms of the branching factor b and solution depth d. (4) Space complexity: the maximum amount of memory needed. For example, BFS is complete, optimal when every step costs the same, but uses O(b^d) memory.
key_points: Four criteria: completeness, optimality, time complexity, space complexity
Usually expressed in terms of branching factor b and solution depth d

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: How is the principle of maximum expected utility used to make decisions? Give an example.
reference_answer: For each possible action, list the possible outcomes, the probability of each and its utility (desirability). The expected utility of an action = Σ P(outcome) × U(outcome). A rational agent chooses the action with the highest expected utility. Example: whether to take an umbrella when the chance of rain is 30%; if U(umbrella, rain) = 8, U(umbrella, sun) = 6, U(no umbrella, rain) = 0, U(no umbrella, sun) = 10, then EU(umbrella) = 0.3·8 + 0.7·6 = 6.6 and EU(no umbrella) = 0.3·0 + 0.7·10 = 7, so choose not to take the umbrella.
key_points: Expected utility = Σ probability × utility of each outcome
A rational agent chooses the action with the highest expected utility

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Why logistic regression does not use MSE loss
question: Why does logistic regression use log-loss (binary cross-entropy) instead of mean squared error (MSE) as in linear regression?
reference_answer: Combining MSE with the sigmoid makes the cost function NON-CONVEX in the parameters, with many local minima and flat regions, so Gradient Descent can get stuck. Moreover, when the sigmoid saturates (confidently wrong predictions, e.g., output near 0 when the label is 1), the MSE gradient contains a very small factor σ'(z), so learning almost stops. Log-loss L = -[y·log(p) + (1-y)·log(1-p)] gives a CONVEX cost in the parameters (guaranteeing a unique global minimum), a simple gradient (p - y)·x not killed by σ'(z), and a probabilistic foundation: minimizing log-loss is exactly maximum likelihood estimation for a Bernoulli distribution.
key_points: MSE + sigmoid gives a non-convex cost and vanishing gradients when the sigmoid saturates
Log-loss is convex, has gradient (p - y)·x, and corresponds to maximum likelihood

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: The normal equation vs Gradient Descent
question: Linear regression can be solved directly with the normal equation θ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy. Compare it with Gradient Descent and state when to use each.
reference_answer: The normal equation gives the exact solution in one step, with no learning rate or iterations and no need for feature scaling; but it requires inverting an n×n matrix (n = number of features) costing about O(n³) time and O(n²) memory, so it is very slow for large n (tens of thousands of features); and XᵀX may be singular when features are linearly dependent or there are more features than samples (requiring a pseudo-inverse or regularization). Gradient Descent needs a learning rate, many iterations and preferably feature scaling, but scales well to large n and m, supports online/mini-batch learning, and applies to any model without a closed-form solution (logistic regression, neural networks). Typically use the normal equation for small n (under a few thousand), Gradient Descent for very large n or data.
key_points: Normal equation: exact one-step solution but O(n³) and possibly singular
Gradient Descent: needs a learning rate and iterations, but scales and works for models without closed forms

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: How does adding polynomial features (x², x³, x1·x2...) to linear regression affect model capacity? Analyze the risks of increasing the polynomial degree.
reference_answer: The model remains linear in its PARAMETERS but becomes non-linear in the original inputs, so it can fit curved relationships and more complex decision boundaries — capacity increases. As the degree grows: (1) overfitting becomes likely — a degree-15 model may pass through every training point but oscillate wildly between them and predict poorly outside the data range; (2) the number of features grows combinatorially (about C(n+d, d) for n features and degree d), costing computation; (3) features like x, x², x³ have very different scales and strong correlations, requiring scaling. Choose the degree with a validation set/cross-validation and combine with regularization.
key_points: Polynomial features increase capacity, fitting non-linear relationships while staying linear in parameters
High degrees cause overfitting, feature explosion and scale disparities; choose by cross-validation with regularization

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Grid search and random search for hyperparameters
question: Compare grid search and random search for hyperparameter tuning. Why is random search often more efficient for the same budget?
reference_answer: Grid search tries every combination of a discrete set of values for each hyperparameter; the number of combinations grows exponentially with the number of hyperparameters. Random search samples combinations randomly from predefined distributions. In practice only a few hyperparameters really matter (Bergstra & Bengio). With a 3×3 grid = 9 trials, each hyperparameter is tried with only 3 distinct values; with 9 random trials, each hyperparameter gets 9 distinct values — exploring the important dimension much more thoroughly. Random search is also easy to stop at any time and to parallelize. Hyperparameters like the learning rate should be sampled on a log scale (10^-5 to 10^-1). Even better methods: Bayesian optimization, Hyperband (early-stopping poor configurations).
key_points: Grid tries all combinations, exploding with the number of hyperparameters; random samples them
Since few hyperparameters matter, random search tries more distinct values per dimension; sample on a log scale

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Choosing a classification threshold by error costs
question: A cancer screening model outputs probabilities. Why should the default threshold of 0.5 not be used, and how should the threshold be chosen?
reference_answer: A 0.5 threshold is only reasonable when both types of errors cost the same and the probabilities are well calibrated. In cancer screening, missing a patient (FN) can be fatal, while a false alarm (FP) only leads to further tests — FN costs far more, so the threshold should be lowered to increase Recall, accepting lower Precision. Conversely, spam filtering should use a high threshold because blocking an important email (FP) is worse than letting spam through. How to choose: determine the cost of each error type and pick the threshold minimizing expected total cost on the validation set; or pick the threshold meeting a minimum requirement (Recall ≥ 95%) with the highest possible Precision, based on the Precision-Recall curve. The threshold must be chosen on the validation set, not the test set.
key_points: A 0.5 threshold only makes sense when both error types cost the same
Choose the threshold by error costs (lower it when misses are dangerous), using the validation set and PR curve

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: ROC-AUC and PR-AUC with imbalanced data
question: For fraud detection (fraud rate 0.1%), why can ROC-AUC give an optimistic impression, and how does PR-AUC reflect performance better?
reference_answer: ROC uses FPR = FP / (FP + TN) on the x-axis. When the negative class is huge (99.9%), TN is enormous so even thousands of false alarms barely raise FPR — the ROC curve still looks great (AUC 0.98) even though most flagged transactions are false alarms. The Precision-Recall curve uses Precision = TP / (TP + FP), independent of TN, directly reflecting the proportion of correct alerts — what fraud investigation teams really care about. PR-AUC's baseline equals the positive class rate (0.001) rather than ROC-AUC's 0.5, so model improvements are more visible. When the positive class is rare and important, report PR-AUC (or Precision at a fixed Recall) alongside ROC-AUC.
key_points: With a huge negative class, many FPs barely raise FPR so ROC-AUC looks optimistic
PR-AUC is based on Precision, independent of TN, with baseline equal to the positive rate; suited for rare positives

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Compare two ways of extending binary classifiers to multi-class problems: One-vs-Rest (OvR) and softmax (multinomial) regression.
reference_answer: OvR trains K independent binary classifiers, the k-th distinguishing 'class k' from 'all other classes'; prediction picks the class with the highest score. Pros: simple, works with any binary classifier (SVM), easy to parallelize. Cons: scores of different classifiers are not jointly calibrated so they are hard to compare, each classifier faces imbalanced data (1 class vs K - 1 classes), and ambiguous regions can exist. Softmax trains ONE joint model with K weight vectors, optimizing cross-entropy, outputting a consistent probability distribution summing to 1 — suited when classes are mutually exclusive. If a sample can have several labels at once (multi-label, e.g., an image with both a cat and a dog), use K independent sigmoids instead of softmax.
key_points: OvR: K independent binary classifiers, simple but scores not jointly calibrated, imbalanced
Softmax: one joint model giving a consistent probability distribution; multi-label needs K sigmoids

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: What does Batch Normalization do inside a neural network and what benefits does it bring?
reference_answer: For each mini-batch, BatchNorm normalizes a layer's inputs (per feature/channel) to zero mean and unit variance using batch statistics, then multiplies by a learnable γ and adds a learnable β so the network can still represent arbitrary distributions. At inference, it uses running mean and variance accumulated during training instead of batch statistics. Benefits: stabilizes activation distributions across layers, allows larger learning rates, faster and more stable training, less sensitivity to weight initialization, and a mild regularization effect from batch-statistic noise. Limitations: depends on batch size (small batches give noisy statistics), so sequence models/Transformers usually use Layer Normalization.
key_points: Normalizes activations by batch statistics, then rescales with learnable γ, β; inference uses running statistics
Faster, stable training, larger learning rates, mild regularization; depends on batch size

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: How do Momentum and Adam improve on plain Gradient Descent?
reference_answer: Momentum maintains a 'velocity', a weighted moving average of past gradients: v ← β·v + ∇J, θ ← θ - α·v. It accelerates when gradients consistently point the same way and dampens oscillation in directions where gradients keep changing sign (narrow valleys), like a ball rolling with inertia. Adam combines momentum (a moving average of the gradient, first moment) with RMSProp (a moving average of squared gradients), dividing the update by the square root of the latter — so each parameter has its own adaptive learning rate: parameters with large/noisy gradients take smaller steps, rarely updated parameters relatively larger ones; plus bias correction in early steps. Adam converges fast with little tuning and is a popular default, although SGD + momentum sometimes generalizes better.
key_points: Momentum accumulates velocity from past gradients, accelerating in stable directions and damping oscillations
Adam combines momentum with per-parameter adaptive learning rates (RMSProp) and bias correction

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Why must the weights of a multi-layer neural network not all be initialized to 0 (or to the same value)? What additional problem do initialization schemes like Xavier/He solve?
reference_answer: If all weights are equal, every neuron in a layer receives the same input, computes the same output and gets the same gradient during backpropagation, so after every update they REMAIN identical — a network with 100 hidden neurons behaves like 1 neuron (the symmetry problem). Random initialization breaks symmetry so neurons learn different features. However, the scale also matters: too large makes activations explode or saturate, too small makes signals and gradients vanish across many layers. Xavier/Glorot (variance ≈ 1/n_in, suited for tanh/sigmoid) and He (variance ≈ 2/n_in, suited for ReLU) choose the scale to keep activation and gradient variances stable across layers.
key_points: Equal weights make neurons in a layer receive equal gradients and stay identical (symmetry)
Random initialization breaks symmetry; Xavier/He choose variances to keep signals and gradients stable

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: What is the 'dying ReLU' phenomenon, its cause and its fix?
reference_answer: ReLU(z) = max(0, z) has zero gradient when z < 0. If after a large update step (too high a learning rate) or poor initialization a neuron's bias becomes very negative so that z < 0 for EVERY input, the neuron always outputs 0 and always has zero gradient — it is never updated again, 'dead' forever. A large fraction of dead neurons reduces network capacity. Fixes: use a smaller learning rate or a decay schedule, proper He initialization, and variants with non-zero gradient in the negative region: Leaky ReLU (max(0.01z, z)), PReLU (learnable negative slope), ELU, GELU. Monitoring the fraction of always-zero neurons helps detect the problem.
key_points: ReLU has zero gradient for z < 0; a neuron with z < 0 for all inputs is never updated again
Fix with a sensible learning rate, He initialization, and Leaky ReLU/PReLU/ELU/GELU

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: What problem do residual (skip) connections in ResNet solve when training very deep networks?
reference_answer: Experiments showed that deeper 'plain' networks (e.g., 56 layers) have HIGHER TRAINING error than shallower ones (20 layers) — not due to overfitting but due to optimization difficulty (the degradation problem): a deep network could in principle be at least as good as a shallow one by having the extra layers learn the identity function, but in practice learning the identity through many non-linear layers is hard. A residual connection makes a block's output y = F(x) + x: the layers only need to learn the residual F(x) = H(x) - x, and if the identity is optimal they just push F toward 0 — much easier. The shortcut also lets gradients flow directly through the addition to early layers without being multiplied through many matrices, mitigating vanishing gradients. This enables training networks with hundreds of layers; the idea also appears in Transformers.
key_points: Deep plain networks are hard to optimize (degradation), with higher training error than shallow ones
y = F(x) + x: learning the residual is easier, gradients flow through the shortcut; enables hundreds of layers

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Parameter counts: convolutional vs fully connected layers
question: For a 224×224×3 input image, compare the number of parameters of (a) a fully connected layer with 1,000 neurons and (b) a convolutional layer with 64 filters of size 3×3. Draw conclusions.
reference_answer: (a) Fully connected: each neuron connects to every input value: 224 × 224 × 3 = 150,528 inputs, times 1,000 neurons ≈ 150.5 million weights (plus 1,000 biases). (b) Convolution: each filter has 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 weights + 1 bias = 28 parameters, 64 filters = 1,792 parameters — about 84,000 times fewer. Meaning: convolution exploits two assumptions suited to images — local connectivity (features depend on neighboring regions) and weight sharing (the same edge detector is useful everywhere) — drastically reducing parameters, reducing overfitting, needing less data and providing translation equivariance. A convolutional layer's parameter count does not depend on the image size.
key_points: Fully connected ≈ 150 million parameters; 64 convolutional 3×3×3 filters only 1,792
Thanks to local connectivity and weight sharing; parameter count independent of image size

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Why do the cell state and forget gate of an LSTM help gradients propagate across many time steps better than a simple RNN?
reference_answer: In a simple RNN, h_t = tanh(W·h_(t-1) + ...): backpropagating through T steps multiplies the gradient repeatedly by the matrix W and the tanh derivative (≤ 1), so it usually shrinks exponentially — distant information cannot influence learning. In an LSTM, the cell is updated mainly by ADDITION: c_t = f_t ⊙ c_(t-1) + i_t ⊙ c̃_t. The derivative of c_t with respect to c_(t-1) is the forget gate f_t (element-wise), not passing through matrix multiplication and squashing functions. When the network learns to keep f_t near 1 for information worth remembering, gradients can flow through hundreds of steps almost undiminished (the constant error carousel). LSTMs do not fully eliminate the problem for very long sequences and computation remains sequential, motivating attention mechanisms.
key_points: Simple RNNs repeatedly multiply by matrices and tanh derivatives, shrinking gradients exponentially
The LSTM cell updates additively; its step derivative is the forget gate, so keeping f near 1 lets gradients flow far

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: On what hypothesis does Word2Vec learn word embeddings? Distinguish the Skip-gram and CBOW architectures.
reference_answer: It relies on the distributional hypothesis: words appearing in similar contexts have similar meanings. Word2Vec trains a shallow network on a prediction task over a context window, and the learned weights are the embedding vectors. CBOW (Continuous Bag-of-Words): predicts the TARGET word from the surrounding context words (averaging context vectors) — trains fast, good for frequent words. Skip-gram: uses the target word to predict EACH context word — slower but represents rare words better. Negative sampling replaces the full softmax for efficient training over large vocabularies. The results show interesting linear relationships such as king - man + woman ≈ queen. Limitation: each word has a single vector regardless of context (polysemy).
key_points: Distributional hypothesis: words with similar contexts have similar meanings
CBOW predicts the target from context (fast); Skip-gram predicts context from the target (better for rare words); one vector per word

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: How does TF-IDF compute the weight of a word in a document and why is it better than raw term frequency?
reference_answer: TF (term frequency) is the word's frequency in the document; IDF (inverse document frequency) = log(N / number of documents containing the word), with N the total number of documents. TF-IDF = TF × IDF. Using frequency alone, common words like 'and', 'of', 'is' always get high weights even though they carry no discriminative information. IDF lowers the weight of words appearing in most documents and raises the weight of rare words specific to a few documents. Thus TF-IDF highlights distinctive keywords, used in document retrieval, keyword extraction and as features for text classification. Limitation: still a bag of words, without understanding semantics or synonyms.
key_points: TF-IDF = term frequency in the document × log(N / documents containing the term)
Down-weights ubiquitous words, highlights distinctive ones; still no semantic understanding

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: How does a bigram language model estimate the probability of a sentence? Why is smoothing needed?
reference_answer: An n-gram model assumes a word's probability depends only on the previous n - 1 words (the Markov assumption). For bigrams: P(sentence) ≈ Π P(w_i | w_(i-1)), where P(w_i | w_(i-1)) = count(w_(i-1), w_i) / count(w_(i-1)) estimated from a corpus. Problem: many valid word pairs do not appear in the training data, so their estimate is 0 and the whole sentence gets probability 0 — the model cannot handle new sentences. Smoothing redistributes some probability mass to unseen events: Laplace (add 1 to every count, simple but crude), Good-Turing, backoff/interpolation (use unigrams when bigram data is lacking), Kneser-Ney (most effective in practice). Language models are evaluated by perplexity on a test set.
key_points: Bigram: P(sentence) = Π P(w_i | w_(i-1)) estimated by counting
Unseen pairs give probability 0; smoothing (Laplace, backoff, Kneser-Ney) assigns mass to unseen events

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: When generating text (e.g., machine translation) from a sequence-to-sequence model, compare greedy decoding and beam search.
reference_answer: Greedy decoding picks the highest-probability token at each step; fast but may miss the best overall sequence because a locally good choice can lead to poor later steps. Beam search keeps the B best partial sequences (by total log-probability) at each step; each is extended with every possible token, then the B best are selected again, until completion. B = 1 is greedy decoding. Beam search usually gives better translations at roughly B times the cost. Notes: total log-probability favors short sentences, so length normalization is needed; for open-ended generation (stories, dialogue), beam search tends to produce repetitive, bland text, so sampling methods are usually used.
key_points: Greedy picks the best token each step: fast but may miss the best sequence
Beam search keeps the B best sequences; needs length normalization; sampling is used for open-ended generation

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: How do the temperature parameter and top-p (nucleus) sampling control text generation by a language model?
reference_answer: Temperature T divides the logits before softmax: p_i ∝ exp(z_i / T). T < 1 makes the distribution 'sharper' — the model picks high-probability tokens, output is stable and less creative (T → 0 is almost greedy); T > 1 makes it 'flatter' — more diverse and creative but more likely to drift off-topic and err. Top-p: sample only from the smallest set of tokens whose total probability ≥ p (e.g., 0.9), discarding the 'long tail' of very unlikely tokens that cause nonsense; the set size adapts to the model's certainty at each step (unlike top-k with a fixed k). For tasks needing precision (extraction, code, factual answers) use low temperature; for creative writing use higher temperature with top-p.
key_points: Temperature scales logits: low is stable, high is diverse but error-prone
Top-p samples from the smallest token set with total probability ≥ p, cutting the long tail and adapting to certainty

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: A company wants a chatbot answering from frequently updated internal documents. Compare two approaches: fine-tuning a model on the documents and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).
reference_answer: RAG: store documents in a search index (usually a vector database); for each question, retrieve the relevant passages and put them into the prompt so the model answers based on them. Pros: updating knowledge only requires updating the index, sources can be cited, hallucinations are reduced, per-document access control is possible, low cost. Cons: quality depends on retrieval, bounded by the context window. Fine-tuning: update model weights with proprietary data. Pros: can teach style, format, terminology, specialized behavior. Cons: costly and requires retraining whenever documents change, knowledge 'baked' into weights is less reliable (still hallucinates, hard to trace sources), and information is hard to remove. For frequently changing knowledge, RAG fits better; the two can be combined (fine-tune for style, RAG for knowledge).
key_points: RAG: retrieve documents into the prompt; easy updates, citable, depends on retrieval quality
Fine-tuning: teaches style/behavior, costly, hard to update and trace; both can be combined

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: What is chain-of-thought prompting and why does it improve language model results on multi-step problems?
reference_answer: Chain-of-thought asks (or demonstrates via examples) the model to write out intermediate reasoning steps before giving the final answer, instead of answering immediately. For multi-step problems (math word problems, logical reasoning), the model generates text token by token: writing intermediate steps lets it 'use' the generated tokens as working memory, decomposing the problem and performing more computation steps before concluding, rather than compressing all reasoning into the single step of producing the answer. The written steps also help humans check the work. Caveats: the written chain is not guaranteed to faithfully reflect the internal process, and it may contain wrong steps leading to wrong conclusions.
key_points: Ask the model to write intermediate reasoning steps before answering
Intermediate tokens act as working memory, allowing more computation; not guaranteed faithful or correct

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: The BLEU metric and its limitations
question: How does the BLEU metric evaluate machine translation quality and what are its limitations?
reference_answer: BLEU compares the machine translation with one or more human reference translations based on n-gram precision (typically n = 1 to 4): the proportion of n-grams in the machine output appearing in the reference (with clipped counts), combined by geometric mean and multiplied by a brevity penalty to stop overly short translations from scoring high. Limitations: only surface word matching, not recognizing synonyms and paraphrases that are correct in meaning; poor assessment of grammar and fluency; weak correlation with human judgment at the sentence level; dependence on the number and quality of references. So today it is supplemented with embedding-based metrics (BERTScore, COMET) and human evaluation.
key_points: BLEU measures n-gram precision against references with a brevity penalty
Surface matching only, misses synonyms, weak sentence-level correlation; supplement with BERTScore/COMET and humans

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Describe the value iteration algorithm for finding the optimal policy of an MDP when the environment model is known.
reference_answer: Initialize V(s) = 0 for all states. Repeatedly apply the Bellman optimality update to every state: V(s) ← max_a Σ_s' P(s' | s, a)·[R(s, a, s') + γ·V(s')], i.e., the value of s is the best result over all actions, based on the immediate reward and the (discounted) value of the next state. With γ < 1 the update is a contraction mapping, so V converges to the optimal value V*; stop when the largest change falls below a threshold. The optimal policy is then extracted: π*(s) = argmax_a Σ_s' P(s' | s, a)·[R + γ·V*(s')]. Each iteration costs O(|S|²·|A|). It requires knowing P and R (model-based planning), unlike Q-learning which learns from experience.
key_points: Iterate the Bellman optimality update V(s) ← max_a Σ P·[R + γV(s')] until convergence
Extract the policy by argmax; needs the model P, R; each sweep costs O(|S|²·|A|)

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Which steps make up policy iteration and how does it differ from value iteration?
reference_answer: Policy iteration alternates two steps: (1) Policy evaluation — for the current policy π, compute V^π by solving the linear Bellman system V(s) = Σ P(s' | s, π(s))·[R + γ·V(s')] (directly or iteratively to convergence); (2) Policy improvement — for each state, choose the action greedy with respect to V^π. Repeat until the policy no longer changes; the resulting policy is optimal. Difference: each policy iteration round is more expensive (fully evaluating a policy) but usually converges in VERY FEW rounds; each value iteration round is cheap (a single Bellman update with max) but needs many rounds. Modified policy iteration evaluates only a few steps, sitting in between.
key_points: Policy iteration: full policy evaluation then greedy improvement, until the policy stops changing
Each round is costlier but converges in few rounds; value iteration rounds are cheap but many

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: SARSA and Q-learning are both temporal-difference (TD) algorithms. How do their update rules and behaviors differ, illustrated with the 'cliff walking' problem?
reference_answer: SARSA (on-policy) updates Q(s, a) ← Q(s, a) + α[r + γ·Q(s', a') - Q(s, a)], where a' is the action ACTUALLY chosen in s' by the current policy (even when exploring randomly). Q-learning (off-policy) uses max_a' Q(s', a') — assuming the best action will be chosen next. In cliff walking with an ε-greedy policy: Q-learning learns the optimal path right along the cliff edge (shortest), but during learning, random exploration often makes it fall off, so its average reward while learning is low. SARSA accounts for its own random exploration and learns a safer path away from the edge, earning higher actual reward while learning. As ε decays to 0, both converge to the optimal policy.
key_points: SARSA uses Q(s', a') of the action actually chosen (on-policy); Q-learning uses the max (off-policy)
Cliff walking: Q-learning learns the edge path but falls during exploration; SARSA picks a safer path

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Compare Monte Carlo and Temporal-Difference (TD) methods for estimating value functions.
reference_answer: Monte Carlo waits until the end of an episode, then updates V(s) toward the actual total return G_t received from s to the end. Pros: unbiased estimates, no strict reliance on the Markov property. Cons: high variance (G_t depends on many random actions and events), only for episodic problems, must wait until the end to learn. TD (e.g., TD(0)) updates right after each step toward r + γ·V(s') — using the current estimate of the next state (bootstrapping). Pros: online step-by-step learning, applicable to continuing tasks, lower variance, usually converges faster. Cons: biased because it relies on imprecise estimates. TD(λ) and n-step TD lie between the two extremes.
key_points: Monte Carlo updates toward the actual end-of-episode return: unbiased, high variance, needs episodes to end
TD updates each step via bootstrapping r + γV(s'): low variance, online, but biased

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: A Bayesian network has two causes, Burglary and Earthquake, both pointing to Alarm. Explain the 'explaining away' phenomenon when we know the alarm rang and then learn there was an earthquake.
reference_answer: Initially Burglary and Earthquake are independent. Observing that the Alarm rang increases the probability of BOTH causes. If we then learn there was an Earthquake, the earthquake already 'explains' why the alarm rang, so the probability of Burglary DROPS (back near its prior) — even though burglaries and earthquakes have no causal link. That is, two independent causes become DEPENDENT when their common effect is observed (a 'v-structure' or collider). This contrasts with chains and forks, where observing the middle variable blocks the flow of influence. Understanding this matters for inference (d-separation) and warns about selection bias: selecting data based on a common effect can create spurious correlations between two independent factors.
key_points: Two independent causes become dependent when their common effect is observed (collider)
Knowing one cause lowers the probability of the other; relevant to d-separation and selection bias

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Approximate inference by sampling: rejection sampling and likelihood weighting
question: When exact inference in a Bayesian network is too expensive, P(X | evidence) can be estimated by sampling. Compare rejection sampling and likelihood weighting.
reference_answer: Rejection sampling: generate complete samples from the network in topological order (each variable sampled from its conditional probability given its parents), DISCARD samples inconsistent with the evidence, then estimate P(X | e) as the proportion among the remaining samples. Simple and unbiased, but when the evidence is rare (probability 0.001), almost every sample is rejected — enormous waste. Likelihood weighting: FIX the evidence variables to their observed values and sample only the others; each sample is weighted by the product of the probabilities of the evidence values given their parents (how 'plausible' the evidence is). No samples are wasted, far more efficient, but when evidence is at 'downstream' nodes, sample weights can become highly uneven, degrading estimate quality. MCMC methods like Gibbs sampling address this further.
key_points: Rejection sampling: generate full samples and discard those inconsistent with evidence; wasteful with rare evidence
Likelihood weighting: fix evidence and weight samples by likelihood; more efficient but weights may be uneven

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: The Viterbi algorithm for Hidden Markov Models
question: Which problem does the Viterbi algorithm solve on a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) and how does it work?
reference_answer: Viterbi finds the most likely SEQUENCE OF HIDDEN STATES generating a given observation sequence, e.g., the part-of-speech tags of a sentence, or the phoneme sequence of a speech signal. It is dynamic programming: δ_t(j) = the highest probability of any state sequence ending in state j at time t and generating the observations up to t; δ_t(j) = max_i [δ_(t-1)(i)·P(j | i)]·P(o_t | j), while storing a back-pointer to the state i achieving the max. At the end, choose the state with the largest δ and follow back-pointers to recover the whole sequence. Complexity O(T·N²) instead of O(N^T) for trying every sequence. In practice log-probabilities are used (adding instead of multiplying) to avoid underflow. Unlike the Forward algorithm (summing over all sequences), Viterbi uses max instead of sum.
key_points: Viterbi finds the most probable hidden state sequence for an observation sequence
DP with δ_t(j) = max_i δ_(t-1)(i)·P(j|i)·P(o_t|j) and back-pointers; O(T·N²), using log-probabilities

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Kalman filters and particle filters both estimate hidden states over time (e.g., a robot's position from noisy sensors). How do they differ in assumptions and in how they represent beliefs?
reference_answer: Both repeat two steps: prediction (using the motion model to forecast the next state) and update (adjusting with the new observation). The Kalman filter assumes a LINEAR system and GAUSSIAN noise, so the belief is always a Gaussian represented by a mean and covariance; updates have closed forms, are very fast and optimal under those assumptions (EKF/UKF variants approximate mildly non-linear systems). A particle filter represents the belief with a large set of weighted SAMPLES (particles): move each particle with the noisy motion model, weight it by how well it matches the observation, then resample. It handles arbitrary non-linear systems and multimodal distributions (the robot could be in one of two identical corridors), but costs more computation and needs enough particles, especially in high-dimensional state spaces.
key_points: Both repeat predict and update; Kalman assumes linear + Gaussian, represented by mean and covariance
Particle filters use weighted samples, handling non-linearity and multimodality at higher computational cost

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: The resolution rule in propositional logic
question: Describe the resolution rule and how it is used to prove KB ⊨ α by refutation.
reference_answer: Resolution rule: from two clauses containing complementary literals, e.g., (A ∨ B) and (¬B ∨ C), infer a new clause of the remaining literals (A ∨ C). To prove KB ⊨ α: convert KB ∧ ¬α to conjunctive normal form (CNF) — a set of clauses; repeatedly apply resolution to pairs of clauses to generate new ones. If the EMPTY clause is derived (a contradiction, e.g., resolving P and ¬P), then KB ∧ ¬α is unsatisfiable, i.e., KB ⊨ α. If no new clauses can be generated and the empty clause has not appeared, α does not follow from KB. Resolution is sound and refutation-complete for propositional logic, but can be exponentially expensive.
key_points: Resolution: (A ∨ B) and (¬B ∨ C) yield (A ∨ C)
Prove KB ⊨ α by converting KB ∧ ¬α to CNF and resolving to the empty clause

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Converting formulas to conjunctive normal form (CNF)
question: Present the steps to convert the formula (A ⇔ B) ⇒ C into conjunctive normal form (CNF).
reference_answer: General steps: (1) eliminate ⇔: P ⇔ Q becomes (P ⇒ Q) ∧ (Q ⇒ P); (2) eliminate ⇒: P ⇒ Q becomes ¬P ∨ Q; (3) push negations inward with De Morgan's laws and double-negation elimination, so ¬ only precedes variables; (4) distribute ∨ over ∧. Applying: (A ⇔ B) ⇒ C = ¬[(¬A ∨ B) ∧ (¬B ∨ A)] ∨ C = [(A ∧ ¬B) ∨ (B ∧ ¬A)] ∨ C. Distributing: (A ∧ ¬B) ∨ (B ∧ ¬A) = (A ∨ B) ∧ (A ∨ ¬A) ∧ (¬B ∨ B) ∧ (¬B ∨ ¬A) = (A ∨ B) ∧ (¬A ∨ ¬B) (dropping tautological clauses). Adding C: (A ∨ B ∨ C) ∧ (¬A ∨ ¬B ∨ C). Note that distribution can blow up the formula exponentially; the Tseitin transformation adds auxiliary variables to keep linear size (equisatisfiable).
key_points: Steps: eliminate ⇔, eliminate ⇒, push ¬ inward (De Morgan), distribute ∨ over ∧
Result (A ∨ B ∨ C) ∧ (¬A ∨ ¬B ∨ C); distribution may blow up, Tseitin keeps linear size

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: What is unification in first-order logic? Find the most general unifier of Knows(John, x) and Knows(y, Mother(y)).
reference_answer: Unification finds a substitution of variables making two expressions identical; it is the core operation of FOL inference (generalized modus ponens, first-order resolution). For Knows(John, x) and Knows(y, Mother(y)): the first argument gives y/John; substituting, the second argument becomes x and Mother(John), giving x/Mother(John). The most general unifier (MGU) is {y/John, x/Mother(John)}. The MGU is the 'least constraining' substitution — every other unifier is an instance of it. An 'occurs check' is needed: x cannot be unified with F(x) because it would create an infinite expression. Expressions like Knows(John, x) and Knows(x, Elizabeth) require renaming variables first (standardizing apart) to be unifiable.
key_points: Unification finds a variable substitution making expressions identical; the MGU is the most general
Example MGU = {y/John, x/Mother(John)}; needs an occurs check and renaming of shared variables

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: What is a Horn clause and why do many practical inference systems (like Prolog, rule engines) restrict knowledge to Horn form?
reference_answer: A Horn clause is a clause with AT MOST ONE positive literal, equivalent to the rule form 'P1 ∧ P2 ∧ ... ∧ Pn ⇒ Q' (a definite clause), or a fact Q, or a constraint consisting only of negative literals. Inference over a Horn knowledge base by forward or backward chaining takes LINEAR time in the size of the knowledge base (in propositional logic), whereas general inference is NP-complete. The rule form is also natural for humans. Prolog is based on first-order Horn clauses with depth-first backward chaining. Trade-off: loss of expressiveness — disjunctive knowledge like 'A ∨ B' (one is true but unknown which) cannot be written directly; Prolog also uses 'negation as failure' (a closed-world assumption).
key_points: A Horn clause has at most one positive literal, equivalent to the rule P1 ∧ ... ∧ Pn ⇒ Q
Linear-time inference instead of NP-complete; trades disjunctive expressiveness; Prolog uses backward chaining

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Compare planning by forward search (progression, from the initial state) and backward search (regression, from the goal) in state space.
