subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Label delay in concept drift detection
question: A credit card fraud detection model: 'fraud' labels are only confirmed when cardholders complain, on average 45-60 days after the transaction. Fraudsters change tactics. Analyze the challenges for monitoring and retraining, and the response strategies.
reference_answer: With delayed labels, real performance metrics (precision, recall) can only be computed for data from 1-2 months ago; by the time a recall drop is detected, the new tactic has caused damage throughout that period. Moreover, labels are biased: transactions blocked by the model are never known to be truly fraudulent or not (a selective feedback loop), and unreported fraud is mislabeled as legitimate at retraining time if the label waiting window is too short. Concept drift (a changing relationship between features and labels) is hard to detect from input distributions alone. Strategies: monitor early signals (score distributions, feature distributions, alert rates, quick feedback from investigators); use preliminary/weak labels (phone confirmations, expert rules); design label waiting windows for retraining and correct for incomplete labels; reserve a small fraction of transactions for an exploration/random audit policy to obtain unbiased data; combine with unsupervised anomaly detection to catch new tactics; consider online learning with higher weights on recent data.
key_points: Delayed labels mean real metrics are measured months late; labels are biased by blocked transactions and unreported fraud
Monitor early signals, weak labels, label waiting windows, random audits for unbiased data, plus anomaly detection

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: Why do k-NN and other Euclidean-distance-based methods perform poorly on high-dimensional data (e.g., 1,000 raw features), even with lots of data? Analyze distance concentration and remedies.
reference_answer: In high-dimensional spaces with independent features, distances between random pairs of points tend to CONCENTRATE around one value: the ratio (farthest - nearest)/nearest tends to 0 as dimension grows. When all points are 'equally far', the notion of 'nearest neighbor' loses meaning — the nearest neighbor is not significantly more similar than a random point. Meanwhile, to cover the space at a fixed density, the amount of data needed grows exponentially with dimension; most volume lies in the 'shell' of the cube. Irrelevant features add noise to distances, drowning out the important ones. Remedies: real data usually lies on low-dimensional manifolds — reduce dimensionality (PCA, autoencoders), learn representations/embeddings where distance is semantically meaningful (metric learning), select features, use suitable metrics (cosine for sparse vectors/text), scale features. This also explains why approximate nearest neighbor search (ANN) on embeddings still works: good embeddings have low intrinsic dimensionality.
key_points: In high dimensions distances concentrate around one value, so 'nearest' loses meaning; data needs grow exponentially
Remedy with dimensionality reduction, learned embeddings/metric learning, feature selection, suitable metrics; real data has low intrinsic dimension

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: A house price regression model has two features 'area (m²)' and 'area (ft²)' (almost perfectly correlated). One coefficient is +5,000, the other -460, and they change wildly each time the model is retrained on a slightly different sample. Analyze.
reference_answer: This is multicollinearity: when features are nearly linearly dependent, infinitely many coefficient combinations give the same predictions (increasing one coefficient and decreasing the other accordingly), so XᵀX is nearly singular and the least squares solution is very sensitive to noise — huge coefficient variance, signs possibly counterintuitive ('larger area, lower price'). PREDICTIVE ability may still be fine (on data with the same correlation structure), but INTERPRETING each coefficient as 'the individual effect of a feature holding others constant' becomes meaningless, since in reality one feature cannot change while the other stays fixed. Detection: correlation matrices, variance inflation factors (VIF), the matrix condition number. Remedies: drop or merge redundant features, use Ridge regularization (stabilizing coefficients by shrinking them) or Lasso (selecting one in a group), PCA; and be careful using coefficients/feature importances for business or causal conclusions.
key_points: Nearly dependent features make XᵀX nearly singular, so coefficients fluctuate and may flip sign
Predictions may be fine but coefficient interpretation is meaningless; detect with VIF, fix by dropping features, Ridge/Lasso, PCA

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: A 10-bird-species classifier, given a photo of a cat, still answers 'sparrow' with 98% softmax probability. Analyze why softmax probability is not a reliable measure of 'whether the model knows', and methods for detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) data.
reference_answer: Softmax always distributes all probability mass among the known classes — there is no 'none of these' option. ReLU networks have the property that, moving away from the training data region in some direction, logits grow nearly linearly, so softmax becomes increasingly CONFIDENT on increasingly unusual inputs. Cross-entropy training only teaches the model to separate classes from each other, not to recognize unseen regions. Consequences: medical systems or self-driving cars confidently making wrong decisions in new situations. OOD detection methods: use other scores instead of max softmax (energy scores, Mahalanobis distance in feature space, distance to nearest neighbors in the training set); estimate uncertainty with deep ensembles or MC dropout (high disagreement on unusual data); train with auxiliary outlier data (outlier exposure); add an 'other' class/abstention mechanism and route to humans. Evaluate on diverse OOD sets since no method catches every kind of shift.
key_points: Softmax must distribute probability among known classes; ReLU networks grow more confident the farther inputs are from training data
Detect OOD with energy scores, Mahalanobis, feature kNN, ensembles/MC dropout, outlier exposure; abstain and route to humans

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: One team combines 10 neural networks with the same architecture and data, differing only in initialization seed, while another combines 3 different model types (boosted trees, a neural network, logistic regression). Analyze what the benefit of an ensemble depends on.
reference_answer: With M models each having error variance σ² and pairwise error correlation ρ, the variance of their average is ρ·σ² + (1 - ρ)·σ²/M. As M grows, the second term goes to 0 but the term ρ·σ² does NOT decrease: the ensemble's benefit is bounded by how correlated the errors are. Nearly identical models make the same mistakes on the same samples so averaging fixes nothing — benefits diminish quickly. Neural networks with different seeds are in practice still meaningfully diverse (landing in different minima), so deep ensembles usually improve both accuracy and probability calibration, but DIFFERENT model types trained on different data/features (bagging, random feature subsets as in Random Forests) usually have less correlated errors and complement each other better — provided each model is good enough (a very poor model can drag down a uniform average). Trade-offs: inference and operational cost grow with the number of models; the ensemble can be distilled into one model.
key_points: Variance of the average = ρσ² + (1 - ρ)σ²/M: the benefit is bounded by error correlation ρ
Diversity (model types, data, features) lowers ρ; each model must be good enough; costs inference, distillable

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Label noise and its effects on training and evaluation
question: A crowdsourced image dataset has about 8% wrong labels. Analyze the effect of label noise on both training and EVALUATION, and strategies to handle it.
reference_answer: Training: large enough neural networks can fully memorize even wrong labels (experiments show they fit even random labels); they usually learn clean, easy samples first and memorize noisy ones later, so long training hurts generalization. Systematic noise (confusion between similar classes like wolves/huskies) is more harmful than random noise. Evaluation: if the test set also has wrong labels, the measured accuracy is biased and model rankings may be reversed — a model that 'memorizes' the same noise pattern as the test set scores higher; studies have found substantial label error rates in popular benchmarks. Strategies: clean the test set first (expert relabeling, multiple annotators with consensus); detect likely mislabels with confident learning (samples that cross-validated models confidently predict differently from their label); noise-robust loss functions, label smoothing; early stopping; co-teaching (two networks selecting low-loss samples for each other); estimating the noise transition matrix to correct the loss.
key_points: Large networks memorize wrong labels, learning clean samples first then noise; systematic noise is more harmful
Wrong test labels bias metrics and may reverse model rankings; clean the test set, confident learning, robust losses, early stopping

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Pitfalls of saliency maps and feature attributions
question: A team uses saliency maps and SHAP to 'prove' a diagnostic model relies on the lesion area rather than shortcuts. Analyze why such explanations can be misleading.
reference_answer: Gradient-based saliency maps: the 'sanity checks' study (Adebayo et al.) showed some methods produce nearly IDENTICAL maps even when model weights are randomized or labels shuffled — they mainly highlight edges and structures of the input image itself (like an edge detector) rather than reflecting the model's reasoning. Maps are also sensitive to small perturbations and can be manipulated. Humans tend toward confirmation: seeing bright regions near the lesion, they believe the model 'looks at the right place', overlooking that it might use that region plus a marker in the corner. SHAP: with strongly correlated features, 'removing' a feature by substituting values from the marginal distribution creates unrealistic samples, and attribution among correlated features can be arbitrary; Shapley values explain the model, not the real world or causal relationships. Correct practice: test the reliability of the explanation method (randomization tests), test hypotheses with direct interventions (masking the lesion/masking markers and observing prediction changes), evaluate on counterfactual sets breaking shortcuts, and treat explanations as leads for investigation, not proof.
key_points: Some saliency maps barely change when the model is randomized, mainly reflecting image edges; humans are prone to confirmation bias
SHAP with correlated features creates unrealistic samples and arbitrary attributions; use sanity checks, intervention tests, counterfactual sets

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
concept: Safety when granting LLM agents tool access
question: A company gives an LLM agent permission to run commands on servers, access the production database and send emails to 'automatically handle incidents'. Analyze the main risks and principles of safe design.
reference_answer: Risks: (1) Wrong actions due to misunderstanding or 'hallucination' — e.g., deleting data while trying to 'clean up', restarting the wrong service; agent errors can spread quickly because it acts continuously without pause. (2) Manipulation via prompt injection from data it reads (logs, tickets, emails containing malicious commands) to perform unauthorized actions with very high privileges. (3) Irreversible actions (deletion, external emails, money transfers). (4) Sensitive data leakage through tools with outbound connections. (5) Difficult auditing of accountability. Principles: least privilege and narrow scope (read-only accounts, allowlisted commands, sandboxed environments); require human approval for high-impact or irreversible actions (human-in-the-loop) with clear action descriptions; prefer reversible actions and dry runs first; rate and budget limits; treat all content read as untrusted data; full logging for auditing; monitoring and an emergency stop mechanism; gradual rollout starting from test environments.
key_points: Risks: wrong actions spreading fast, prompt injection with high privileges, irreversible actions, data leakage
Least privilege, sandboxing, human approval for major actions, prefer reversibility/dry runs, limits, logging and a kill switch

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: A hospital deploys AI to assist in reading X-rays, more accurate than the average doctor. After a year, doctors' overall diagnostic accuracy with AI assistance has not improved as expected, and doctors miss many cases the AI did not flag. Analyze automation bias and how to design better collaboration.
reference_answer: Automation bias: humans tend to over-trust suggestions of automated systems — accepting wrong suggestions (errors of commission) and becoming less vigilant about what the system does not flag (errors of omission), especially when the system is usually right, under time pressure and when users are tired. Combined with 'deskilling' as humans practice less on their own. As a result, the human + AI team can be worse than the AI alone or fail to exploit complementary strengths, because humans do not know WHEN to trust the AI. Conversely, humans sometimes dismiss the AI right after seeing it fail once (algorithm aversion). Better design: provide calibrated confidence and information about the model's known weaknesses (groups, image types it handles poorly); workflows requiring doctors to read independently before seeing AI suggestions (avoiding anchoring), or the AI acting as a second reader; explanations supporting verification rather than replacing judgment; training users on AI limitations; measuring the performance of the WHOLE human + AI system in practice, not just the AI on a test set; and preserving opportunities for humans to maintain their skills.
key_points: Automation bias: over-trusting suggestions and lowering vigilance for unflagged cases; plus deskilling
Design: calibrated confidence, independent reading before suggestions, training on limitations, measuring whole human + AI performance

subject: Introduction to Artificial Intelligence
question: A company trains a traffic sign classifier on publicly collected and community-contributed data. Analyze the risk of data poisoning attacks creating backdoors, why they are hard to detect, and defenses.
reference_answer: An attacker injects a small number of malicious samples into the training data: 'Stop' sign images with a small distinctive sticker (the trigger) labeled 'Speed limit'. The model learns a hidden rule 'trigger present → predict Speed limit', while performing perfectly on normal data — accuracy on the clean test set does not drop, so the backdoor goes undetected by ordinary evaluation. At deployment, the attacker only needs to put the sticker on a real sign to trigger it. Only a tiny fraction of poisoned samples (under 1%) is needed, and there are 'clean-label' variants — poisoned samples with entirely correct-looking labels — very hard to catch by manual inspection. Similar risks apply to pre-trained models downloaded from untrusted sources and to web data for LLMs. Defenses: control and trace data provenance, restrict/moderate community contributions; detect anomalous samples in feature space (spectral signatures, activation clustering); scan models with trigger-detection techniques (Neural Cleanse); fine-prune on trusted clean data; use signed models from trusted sources; adversarial testing before deployment in safety-critical systems.
key_points: Injecting a few trigger samples with wrong labels creates a backdoor; the model remains good on clean data so normal evaluation misses it
Defenses: data provenance control, anomaly detection in feature space, trigger scanning, fine-pruning, trusted model sources
